title: Classifier training concentrated Qwen3 hallucination signals in middle layers
summary: Researchers fitted linear probes at different stages of classifier-head fine-tuning and found that hallucination labels became readable in a band of Qwen3's upper-middle layers before appearing across later layers. Combining the later layers gave no improvement over a single-layer probe in held-out comparisons. Removing 31% of the layers above the signal-forming band and a stabilization margin preserved detection scores within seed variability in Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B.

source_review.scope: Original arXiv v1 metadata and full-text HTML §§3–6, readout and transfer appendix context

evidence.tested: The authors tracked linear probe performance across network layers and fine-tuning checkpoints. Controlled fusion tests on a six-corpus held-out split looked for complementary upper-layer information. Three-seed depth-truncation comparisons tested what happens when different layers are removed.
evidence.unknown: The findings concern decodable binary hallucination labels in these task-trained models. They do not imply the same depth in other tasks, and measured early-exit scores varied on transfer backbones.
evidence.ai_role: Classifier-head training and fitted linear probes expose where task labels are decodable in the learned models. Comparisons with sequence-to-sequence tuning, fusion probes and layer truncation test whether late-layer signals differ or are redundant for the classification.
